units.title: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
units.kid: Looking at data, and collecting it fairly
units.summary: Every statistical study starts with an [[investigative|investigative question]] and some [[data]]. In this unit you learn to graph one variable, describe it with numbers, and collect data in a fair way.
units.example: Investigative question: “How many minutes do students at our school read each night?” A [[histogram]] for 50 randomly chosen students shows most read 20 to 30 minutes, and one reads 120. That student is an [[outlier]].
ideas: A study starts with an [[investigative|investigative question]] about a group, like “How much sleep do 9th graders at our school get?” Then you name the [[population]], the [[sample]] and the [[variable|variables]].
Is the variable a [[categorical|category]] or a [[quantitative|number]]? Categories go in tables, bar graphs and pie charts. Numbers go in dotplots, [[histogram|histograms]] and [[boxplot|boxplots]].
Describe a graph of numbers by its shape, center, spread and any unusual values, always in the story's words.
Center: the [[mean]] (average) or the [[median]] (middle). Spread: [[sd|standard deviation]], [[iqr|IQR]] or [[range]]. If the data is [[skewed]] or has outliers, the median and IQR are safer.
A [[zscore|z-score]] says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean, so you can compare things on different scales.

Collecting data: a [[census]] asks everyone and a sample asks some. Random samples ([[srs|SRS]], [[stratified|stratified]], [[cluster|cluster]]) help avoid [[bias]]. An [[experiment]] with [[randomassign|random assignment]] can show cause and effect; an [[observational|observational study]] can't.
units.watch: Random sampling and random assignment do different jobs. Sampling is about WHO is in the study, so you can talk about the whole population. Assignment is about WHICH treatment each person gets, so you can talk about cause and effect.
units.ask: What's the difference between random sampling and random assignment?

units.title: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
units.kid: Chance, and the shapes data make
units.summary: [[probability|Probability]] is the math of chance. You'll read [[twoway|two-way tables]], run [[simulation|simulations]], learn the probability rules, and meet three famous shapes: the binomial, the normal curve and sampling distributions.
units.example: A spinner is one-quarter red. Spin it 1,000 times and about 250 spins land on red. That's the [[lawlarge|law of large numbers]].
ideas: Two category variables go in a [[twoway|two-way table]]. Compare percents, not raw counts, to see if they're linked.
A [[simulation]] uses random numbers, like coin flips or a computer, to estimate a probability by trying something many times.
Probability rules: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). “Or”: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). “And” for [[independent]] events: P(A) × P(B). [[conditional|Conditional]]: P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B).
A [[randomvar|random variable]] has an [[expected|expected value]] (its long-run average) and a standard deviation.
[[binomial|Binomial]]: a set number of tries, each one yes or no with the same chance. Count the successes.

The [[normal|normal curve]] and the [[empirical|68–95–99.7 rule]] give percents. A [[samplingdist|sampling distribution]] shows how a statistic changes from sample to sample, and the [[clt|central limit theorem]] says sample means make a bell shape when samples are big.
units.watch: [[mutex|Mutually exclusive]] is not the same as independent. If two things can't happen together, knowing one happened changes the chance of the other a lot.
units.ask: How do I know if something is a binomial setting?

units.title: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
units.summary: Now you use a sample to say something about everyone, like “about 58% of all students want school to start later.” You'll build [[ci|confidence intervals]], run significance tests, and use chi-square tests on two-way tables.
units.example: In a random sample of 200 students, 116 (58%) want a later start. A 95% confidence interval says the true percent is probably between 51% and 65%.
ideas: A good [[statistic]] is [[unbiased]]: it's centered on the truth. The sample proportion p̂ estimates the population proportion p.
A confidence interval is estimate ± [[marginoferror|margin of error]]. For one proportion: p̂ ± z*·√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n). The [[confidencelevel|confidence level]] is how often the method catches the truth.
A significance test asks “could this just be luck?” Write [[hypothesis|hypotheses]] about p, check the [[conditions]], find the [[pvalue|p-value]], and compare it to [[alpha|α]].
Mistakes happen: a [[type1|Type I error]] is a false alarm, a [[type2|Type II error]] is a missed alarm, and [[power]] is the chance of catching a real effect.
Two groups? Use the difference p̂₁ − p̂₂ to estimate or test p₁ − p₂.
Two category variables in a two-way table? A [[chisquare|chi-square]] test for homogeneity or independence checks whether the counts fit the [[expectedcounts|expected counts]] for “no link.”
units.watch: Don't say “there's a 95% chance the true value is in my interval.” Say “We are 95% confident the interval from __ to __ captures the true proportion of __.”
units.ask: What does a p-value actually mean?

units.title: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
units.summary: The same big ideas as Unit 3, but for averages. Because we don't know σ, we use the [[tdist|t-distribution]] instead of z.
units.example: A random sample of 25 batteries lasts 9.6 hours on average. The box says 10 hours. A t-test tells you if 9.6 is too low to blame on luck.
ideas: The sample mean x̄ has a sampling distribution centered at μ, with standard deviation σ/√n. It's about normal if the population is normal or n ≥ 30.
Use t, not z, for means: x̄ ± t*·s/√n, with [[df|df]] = n − 1.
Normal condition: n ≥ 30, OR the population is normal, OR a graph of the sample shows no strong skew or outliers.
[[paired|Paired data]] (the same people measured twice): subtract to get one list of differences, then use one-sample t on the mean difference.
Two separate groups: estimate or test μ₁ − μ₂ with a two-sample t procedure.
Bigger samples and less spread make intervals narrower and tests more [[power|powerful]].
units.watch: Two lists from the same people (before and after) is paired, not two-sample. Ask: is each number in list 1 linked to one number in list 2?
units.ask: How do I tell paired data from two independent samples?

units.title: Regression Analysis
units.summary: Now you look at two number variables at once, like hours of sleep and test scores, and fit a line that predicts one from the other.
units.example: Plot hours studied against test score. The dots climb up and to the right in a fairly straight line, so there's a strong, positive relationship.
ideas: Make a [[scatterplot]] and describe its direction, form, strength and unusual points.
[[correlation|Correlation (r)]] runs from −1 to 1. Near ±1 is strong; near 0 is weak. It only measures straight-line patterns.
A regression line ŷ = a + bx predicts y. Explain the [[slope]] in context: “for each extra hour, the predicted score goes up b points.”
A [[residual]] is actual minus predicted. A residual plot with no pattern means a straight line fits well.
The [[lsrl|least-squares regression line]] makes the squared residuals as small as possible. [[r2|r²]] tells what percent of the change in y the line explains.
Be careful with [[extrapolation]]: predicting far outside your data is risky.
units.watch: Correlation is not causation. Ice cream sales and sunburns rise together, but ice cream doesn't cause sunburns. Hot weather causes both.
units.ask: How do I explain the slope of a regression line in context?
